abstract: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) forms specialized microdomains that organize autophagy, lipid droplet formation, and the repair of damaged lysosomes. The PI3P-binding protein DFCP1/ZFYVE1 marks these microdomains, raising the question as to whether and how one protein could define such a subcompartment. Here we determine the structure of full-length human DFCP1 bound to membranes by cryo-electron tomography and single-particle cryo-electron microscopy. DFCP1 assembles into a helical coat, built from tetramers that stack around a constricted membrane tube. Its ATPase domains form the organizing core of the helix, while its ER-targeting domains insert deeply into the outer leaflet, and its FYVE domains grip PI3P. Coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations show that the coat does not simply follow the curvature of the membrane but acts as a barrier to lipid diffusion, almost completely blocking the movement of its cognate lipid PI3P past the filament and concentrating it beneath the coat. Point mutations that break the assembly, membrane-insertion or PI3P-binding interfaces each impair lysosomal repair in cells, and the assembly is also required for the focal recruitment of the lipid transporter VPS13C. We propose that DFCP1 collars fence off a specialized ER microdomain, so that locally made lipids can reach sites of repair rather than escaping into bulk ER.
